title: The Little-Known Flaw Behind The ‘Failure’ Of The Common Core
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Responding to Tom Loveless's book on the failure of the Common Core, Wexler agrees with some of his conclusions but argues he misses the standards' original flaw. That flaw was equating reading with math: math standards specify content, while literacy standards list generic comprehension skills without saying what students should read. She explains that cognitive science shows comprehension grows with knowledge, so a skills-first reading curriculum marginalises the social studies and science that build it. Language about building knowledge was added to supplementary material after E.D. Hirsch's intervention, but most teachers absorbed only close reading and more nonfiction, and many leaned further into generic skills and leveled texts. She notes a possible silver lining in the growth of content-rich curricula, and concludes that curriculum matters more than standards.
points: The Common Core's original sin was treating literacy like math, listing comprehension skills without specifying the knowledge students must build.
Comprehension depends on background knowledge, so skills-focused instruction and displaced social studies and science undercut the reading scores schools are chasing.
Knowledge-building language sat in supplementary material, so teachers mostly heard close reading and more nonfiction, and surveys show more generic skills instruction and more leveled reading.
Plain nonfiction without background knowledge can yield nothing for children, who previously at least learned from simple fiction.
Content-rich elementary curricula now exist, but Wexler doubts teachers alone will drive change and expects some top-down push is needed.
quotes: I agree with some of Loveless’s conclusions, but he misses some fundamental points about the standards that I gleaned from researching my own book The Knowledge Gap. The fatal flaw—or original sin—of the Common Core was the false equivalence its creators drew between reading and math.

But as evidence from cognitive science indicates—and dismal and stagnant reading scores confirm—comprehension can only develop alongside knowledge. The more you know about a topic, the better able you are to comprehend a text about it. And the more general academic knowledge and vocabulary you have, the better your reading comprehension is in general.

But that language appears in supplementary material, not in the standards themselves; few people are aware of it, and Loveless doesn’t mention it. For most educators, the messages that did come across were that students needed to engage in “close reading” of complex text, and that they needed to read more nonfiction.

Surveys have shown that teachers in Common Core states are actually focusing instruction more on generic skills than they used to, believing that’s what the standards require—even though, in another little-known statement, Coleman and the other lead author of the literacy standards said instruction should focus on questions specific to the text rather than generic “skills” like “finding the main idea.

On a steady diet of simple fiction, which is what elementary students used to get, children without much academic knowledge at least had a chance of understanding the texts and acquiring some new knowledge and vocabulary. But if they’re handed nonfiction for which they have no background knowledge, they may simply get nothing out of it.

A few years ago, it was impossible to buy an elementary literacy curriculum that focused on content; now there are several available, some of them for free. And a relatively small but increasing number of schools and districts are adopting them.
I agree with Loveless that standards are less important than curriculum. But he seems to rely on teachers themselves to initiate change, and I’m skeptical.
